summary: This file is a unittest suite for the new `speak` method that was added to the robot pet classes. Each test sets the pet's battery and mood to a known state, calls `speak()`, and checks that the returned sentence contains the words that state is supposed to produce.

lines.text: Brings in Python's built-in testing framework, which supplies the `TestCase` base class and the assertion methods used throughout the file.

lines.code: from pet_talents import RobotPet, RobotCat, RobotBird, RobotDog
lines.text: Imports the four classes under test from the module that holds the production code, keeping the tests in a separate file from the thing they test.
Each class of pet gets its own `TestCase` class, so a failure report tells you immediately which pet misbehaved.

The ellipsis stands for the `setUp` method shown earlier in the chapter, which runs before every test and creates a fresh pet (here `self.pet`) so that no test can be affected by changes another test made.
Test methods must begin with `test_` for unittest to discover and run them; the rest of the name should describe the situation being checked.
Sets up the condition the test is about by dropping the battery below the low-power threshold, rather than waiting for the pet to run down naturally.

`assertIn` passes when the first value appears somewhere inside the second, so the test checks for the key word instead of the exact sentence — the wording can be polished later without breaking the test.
Covers the second branch of `speak`: a healthy battery combined with a happy mood.
Mood and battery are both set explicitly, because a test that relies on default values silently breaks when those defaults change.
Covers the fall-through branch, the ordinary greeting used when nothing special is going on. Together these three tests exercise every path through `speak`.
Checks a rule that should hold no matter which branch runs: the pet always says its own name.
The cat's low-battery wording differs from the base pet's, which is exactly why each subclass needs its own tests rather than inheriting the parent's.
The searched text may be more than one word; `assertIn` looks for the whole phrase as a substring, capitals included.
This guard is true only when the file is run directly, so importing it elsewhere will not kick off the test run.
Finds every `test_` method in the file, runs each one on a freshly built pet, and prints a summary of passes and failures.
